scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)

meta.presentation: Stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app must SHUFFLE at runtime with a fixed seed so consecutive items do not come from the same axis.

questions.text: A communist party can come to power through elections and hold it without an armed seizure.
Where a parliament exists, contesting it seriously is a better use of cadre than preparing for armed struggle.
A negotiated transfer of power is preferable to civil war, even at the cost of real concessions.
The existing army and police can be won over and reformed rather than smashed.
Signing a peace accord and entering government can be a revolutionary act rather than a capitulation.
A broad electoral alliance with non-communist parties is worth the programmatic compromises it requires.
No ruling class has ever given up state power without being forced, and none ever will.
Building an armed force is the central task of a revolutionary party, not one task among several.
Standing in elections is only ever worthwhile as a way of exposing them.
The standing army and the police must be dismantled outright, never inherited.
A party that has not prepared for illegality will be destroyed the moment it becomes dangerous.
Every peaceful road to socialism attempted so far has ended in the movement's defeat.
The peasantry, not the industrial working class, is the main force of revolution across most of the world.
Revolution advances by building base areas in the countryside and encircling the cities from them.
The land question is the decisive question of the revolution.
In a semi-feudal country the urban proletariat is far too small to lead on its own.
The most reliable cadre are recruited from the villages rather than the factories.
Rural poverty produces a sharper and more durable class hatred than industrial wage labour does.
Only the industrial working class can lead a socialist revolution; other classes can at most follow it.
A revolution with a rural base ends in peasant war, not in proletarian power.
The decisive battles are fought in the cities, where production and the state are concentrated.
Socialism presupposes large-scale industry and the class that large-scale industry creates.
Organising in the workplaces takes priority over organising in the countryside.
What the peasantry wants is land of its own, and that is not a socialist demand.
Once the party has settled a line, no member may argue against it in public.
Organised factions inside the party must be prohibited outright.
The party should be a selected body of tested cadre, not a mass membership open to anyone.
Party decisions must bind lower bodies absolutely, with no appeal to the membership at large.
Ideological uniformity is a source of strength in a revolutionary party, not a weakness.
Removing unreliable elements from the ranks is a normal and necessary part of party life.
The right to form organised tendencies within the party must be permanent and unconditional.
Party leaderships should be openly contested and removable by the membership at any time.
Disagreements inside a revolutionary party should be argued out in public, in front of the class.
Other working-class parties should be free to exist and compete after the revolution.
A party that suppresses internal disagreement will make worse decisions, not better ones.
Trade unions and mass organisations should keep real independence from the party that leads them.
The socialist states of the twentieth century were, on the whole, genuine workers' states worth defending.
Criticism of existing socialist states mainly serves imperialism, whatever the critic intends.
The achievements of the socialist camp outweigh its errors by a wide margin.
Where a socialist state and an imperialist power come into conflict, one takes the socialist side without conditions.
The collapse of the Soviet Union was a defeat for the working class of the entire world.
States that describe themselves as socialist today deserve the movement's active support.
Most states that called themselves socialist had long since stopped being workers' states.
A bureaucratic caste ruled in the name of the working class while excluding it from power.
Defending existing socialist states uncritically has cost the movement more than any enemy has.
Past a certain point the ruling parties of the socialist camp went over to revisionism.
State ownership on its own does not make a country socialist.
The socialist camp should be judged by exactly the standards applied to any other state.
Classes and class struggle persist under socialism and can restore capitalism if they are not fought.
A new bourgeoisie can form inside the ruling party itself.
The masses must be mobilised to criticise and overturn officials, even at the cost of disorder.
Transforming consciousness and social relations matters as much as raising output does.
Periodic upheavals from below are necessary to stop the state from hardening into a caste.
Technical experts and managers become a privileged stratum unless they are constantly checked.
The main task after taking power is developing the productive forces, not further class struggle.
Once the means of production are socialised, the class question is essentially settled.
Mass campaigns against officials disrupt production and set the whole economy back.
Poverty, not insufficient revolutionary consciousness, is the main obstacle to socialism.
Steady administration serves the working class better than permanent upheaval does.
Raising living standards is the strongest argument socialism can make.
Markets and private enterprise can be used for a long period under the direction of a socialist state.
Enterprises should set much of their own output, pricing, and investment.
Foreign investment can be admitted on terms set by a socialist state without endangering it.
Competition between socialist enterprises improves efficiency more than commands from above do.
Some inequality of income is acceptable where it raises overall output.
Self-management of individual enterprises is preferable to direction by central ministries.
The whole economy should follow a single plan, with no market in the means of production.
A durable turn back toward market allocation under socialism risks becoming a slide toward capitalist restoration.
Prices should be set by the plan according to need, not by supply and demand.
Private enterprise should be eliminated altogether, not tolerated in a subordinate role.
Wage differentials should be compressed as far as production allows.
Trade with capitalist countries should be minimised in favour of self-reliance.
Socialism cannot be completed in a single country; it stands or falls internationally.
A socialist state's foreign policy should be subordinated to spreading revolution abroad.
The revolution must be carried forward without pausing at any national stage.
A workers' state that puts its own diplomatic interests first has already begun to degenerate.
Building an international organisation matters more than consolidating any one national party.
Borders are an obstacle the revolution has to dissolve, not a framework to work within.
A single country can build socialism on its own, whatever happens elsewhere.
Self-reliance is the first duty of a revolutionary state; outside assistance is a bonus.
Each country's revolution must follow its own road, determined by its own party.
Exporting revolution wastes resources the country needs to defend and develop itself.
A socialist state should make whatever diplomatic arrangements its security requires.
Loyalty to one's nation and loyalty to the revolution point in the same direction.
A revolution needs one recognised leader whose thought guides the whole movement.
A leader's contribution should be named as a distinct development of Marxism.
Public veneration of the leader strengthens the movement's cohesion.
Where the leader and the central committee disagree, the leader is usually right.
A movement with no authoritative individual leader falls into indecision.
The leader embodies the continuity of the revolution across generations.
No individual should ever be placed above the party's collective bodies.
Structuring the movement's authority around one leader's personal standing, however capable they are, leaves it fragile once that leader is gone.
Naming a doctrine after a living leader is a warning sign, not a theoretical advance.
Leadership positions should rotate and remain accountable to elected bodies.
Theory belongs to the movement as a whole, never to any single thinker.
A leader's personal authority should never exceed the office they hold.
